title: al-Amthila al-mukhtalifa
author: Anonymous
subject: sarf
summary: The Amthila (Turkish Emsile), a short anonymous book of tables that lays out the whole of ṣarf on one verb, naṣara, “to help”. It is the first book of the Ottoman madrasa, learnt by heart before any other and followed by the Binā, the Maqṣūd, al-ʿIzzī and Marāḥ al-arwāḥ, with which it is printed in the Majmūʿat al-ṣarf. It opens with the “varied forms”, one form of each kind recited in a breath, and then gives the “regular forms” of each kind in full: the fourteen persons of the past and the present, active and passive, the maṣdar and the participles, the five negations, command and prohibition, and the nouns derived from the verb. The lessons explain each table, how the madrasa recites it, and how it carries over to other sound verbs, with the forms of the print and of The Nahwi's conjugation tool.

lessons.title: The varied forms: the verb and its family
body: After the basmala the Amthila gives, in one breath, fourteen forms of the verb naṣara, “to help”: naṣara, yanṣuru, naṣran, fa-huwa nāṣirun, wa-dhāka manṣūrun, lam yanṣur, lammā yanṣur, mā yanṣuru, lā yanṣuru, lan yanṣura, li-yanṣur, lā yanṣur, unṣur, lā tanṣur. These are “the varied forms” (al-amthila al-mukhtalifa): each is of a different kind. Every kind comes back later in the book as a full table in all its persons, “the regular forms” (al-amthila al-muṭṭarida). In the Ottoman madrasa the child recites this line until it runs like a song, and every verb he meets afterwards is recited in the same order.

The first five give the verb and its first nouns, joined into a little sentence: “he helped, he helps, a helping; so he is a helper, and that one is helped”. Fa-huwa (“so he is”) and wa-dhāka (“and that one”) are not part of the forms. They make the recital a sentence and show at once that nāṣir describes the one who does the act and manṣūr the one it is done to.

Then come five negations: lam yanṣur, “he did not help”; lammā yanṣur, “he has not yet helped”; mā yanṣuru, “he is not helping”; lā yanṣuru, “he will not help”; lan yanṣura, “he will never help”. Listen to the endings. After lam and lammā the verb ends in sukūn, after mā and lā it keeps its ḍamma, after lan it takes a fatḥa. Ṣarf records these forms; naḥw explains them, as jazm and naṣb after their governors.

Last come four forms of command and prohibition: li-yanṣur, “let him help”, and lā yanṣur, “let him not help”, said of someone absent (ghāʾib); unṣur, “help!”, and lā tanṣur, “do not help!”, said to the one present (ḥāḍir), the person addressed.

Why naṣara? It is the first of the six bābs, the patterns of the bare three-letter verb, in the order of the ṣarf books: faʿala, yafʿulu. One verb is learnt perfectly, and the others follow it by analogy (qiyās). The same line can be made for any sound verb: kataba, yaktubu, fa-huwa kātibun wa-dhāka maktūbun, lam yaktub, lan yaktuba, uktub.

tasks.prompt: Recite the fourteen varied forms of naṣara in the book's order and give the meaning of each.
tasks.answer: Naṣara (he helped), yanṣuru (he helps), naṣran (a helping), fa-huwa nāṣirun (so he is a helper), wa-dhāka manṣūrun (and that one is helped), lam yanṣur (he did not help), lammā yanṣur (he has not yet helped), mā yanṣuru (he is not helping), lā yanṣuru (he will not help), lan yanṣura (he will never help), li-yanṣur (let him help), lā yanṣur (let him not help), unṣur (help!), lā tanṣur (do not help!).

tasks.prompt: Make the first line of the recital for ḍaraba, “to strike” (its maṣdar is ḍarb).
tasks.answer: Ḍaraba, yaḍribu, ḍarban, fa-huwa ḍāribun, wa-dhāka maḍrūbun.

tasks.prompt: Give the negations with lam, lan and mā for kataba, “to write”, and say which change the ending of yaktubu.
tasks.answer: Lam yaktub (the ending becomes a sukūn), lan yaktuba (it becomes a fatḥa), mā yaktubu (no change).

tasks.prompt: Which of the fourteen are said of someone absent, and which to the person addressed?
tasks.answer: Li-yanṣur and lā yanṣur are of the absent (ghāʾib). Unṣur and lā tanṣur are to the one present (ḥāḍir). The others in the line are all of the absent man, the first person of every table.

quiz.prompt: What are “the varied forms” (al-amthila al-mukhtalifa)?
options: All fourteen persons of the past
One form of each kind, recited in one breath
The forms of the passive only
quiz.explanation: Each kind appears once here; the regular forms then give each kind in all its persons.

quiz.prompt: What does naṣara mean?
quiz.explanation: The whole book is built on this one verb, “to help”.

quiz.prompt: In fa-huwa nāṣirun wa-dhāka manṣūrun, what are fa-huwa and wa-dhāka?
options: Two more forms of the verb
Words that make the recital a sentence, not forms
quiz.explanation: They show that nāṣir is the doer, manṣūr the one acted upon.

quiz.prompt: Which negation means “he has not yet helped”?
quiz.explanation: Lammā denies up to now, with the act still expected.

quiz.prompt: After which particle does yanṣuru take a fatḥa?
quiz.explanation: Lan yanṣura: the verb is in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Unṣur, “help!”, is said to…
quiz.explanation: The command to the one present; li-yanṣur is the command to the absent.

quiz.prompt: Why is naṣara the model verb?
options: It is the oldest verb in Arabic
It is the first of the six bābs of the bare verb
quiz.explanation: Faʿala, yafʿulu heads the bābs in the ṣarf books; the others follow by analogy.

lessons.title: The varied forms: the nouns and the wonder
body: The second half of the varied forms gives ten words made from the same root, all but the last two nouns: manṣar, minṣar, naṣra, niṣra, nuṣayr, naṣrī, naṣṣār, anṣar, mā anṣarahu and anṣir bihi. Each is a pattern (wazn) that ṣarf can lay on a root, and the madrasa learns it once, on naṣara, by its weight on faʿala: mafʿal, mifʿal, faʿla, fiʿla, fuʿayl, faʿlī, faʿʿāl, afʿal, mā afʿalahu, afʿil bihi.

The first four name the act in some way. Manṣar (mafʿal) is the time or the place of helping, and also a maṣdar with a mīm, “a helping”. Minṣar (mifʿal) is the instrument, “a thing to help with”. Naṣra (faʿla) is one single act, “one help”; niṣra (fiʿla) the manner, “a way of helping”. Mark the pairs: manṣar and minṣar, naṣra and niṣra, differ by one vowel only, and the vowel is the whole difference.

The next four describe. Nuṣayr (fuʿayl) is the diminutive, “a little help”. Naṣrī, with the ending -iyy, is “related to help”, the relative adjective (nisba), as Makkī is “from Makka”. Naṣṣār (faʿʿāl) is the intensive, “a great helper”, one who helps much. Anṣar (afʿal) is the elative, “more helpful”, “most helpful”.

The last two are the two verbs of wonder (taʿajjub): mā anṣarahu, “how helpful he is!”, and anṣir bihi, which means the same. The second looks like a command, but it is not one; it states one's wonder. In the print it is joined to the line with wa-, as wa-anṣir bihi.

These patterns are given in full for naṣara because the book teaches patterns. Whether the Arabs actually used a diminutive or an instrument of a given verb is a question for the dictionary, not for the Amthila. The fourth part of the book, the derived nouns, gives each of these words its own table.

tasks.prompt: Give the pattern on faʿala and the name of each: nuṣayr, naṣṣār, minṣar, naṣrī, anṣar.
tasks.answer: Nuṣayr: fuʿayl, the diminutive. Naṣṣār: faʿʿāl, the intensive. Minṣar: mifʿal, the instrument. Naṣrī: faʿlī, the relative adjective (nisba). Anṣar: afʿal, the elative.

tasks.prompt: Manṣar and minṣar, naṣra and niṣra: what does each mean, and what alone tells them apart?
tasks.answer: Manṣar: the time or place of helping (or the maṣdar mīmī); minṣar: the instrument. Naṣra: one act of helping; niṣra: a manner of helping. Only the first vowel tells them apart: fatḥa or kasra.

tasks.prompt: Sort the ten into: words that name the act, words that describe, and verbs of wonder.
tasks.answer: Naming the act: manṣar, minṣar, naṣra, niṣra. Describing: nuṣayr, naṣrī, naṣṣār, anṣar. Verbs of wonder: mā anṣarahu, anṣir bihi.

quiz.prompt: What is minṣar?
quiz.explanation: Mifʿal: a thing to help with. Manṣar, with fatḥa, is the time or place.

quiz.prompt: Naṣra and niṣra differ in…
options: their first vowel only: one act against a manner
quiz.explanation: Faʿla is one act (marra); fiʿla the manner (nawʿ).

quiz.prompt: Which form means “a great helper”, one who helps much?
quiz.explanation: Faʿʿāl is the intensive (mubālagha).

quiz.prompt: What does mā anṣarahu express?
quiz.explanation: It is the first verb of wonder (taʿajjub).

quiz.prompt: Anṣir bihi looks like a command. What is it?
quiz.explanation: Its form is that of a command; its meaning is wonder.

quiz.prompt: What is the pattern of nuṣayr?
quiz.explanation: Fuʿayl is the pattern of the diminutive of a three-letter noun.

quiz.prompt: Naṣrī, “related to help”, is made with…
options: an alif after the first letter
quiz.explanation: As Makkī is “from Makka”.

lessons.title: The active past in its fourteen persons
body: Now the regular forms begin, and the first is the active past (al-māḍī al-maʿlūm) in its fourteen persons (ṣiyagh). Every table of the book keeps the same order: three forms of the absent man (one, two, many), three of the absent woman, three of the man addressed, three of the woman addressed, and two of the speaker, alone and with others: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 14.

The madrasa recites each form with its name: naṣara, one man absent (mufrad mudhakkar ghāʾib); naṣarā, two men absent; naṣarū, many men absent; naṣarat, one woman absent; naṣaratā, two women; naṣarna, many women; naṣarta, one man addressed; naṣartumā, two men addressed; naṣartum, many men; naṣarti, one woman addressed; naṣartumā, two women; naṣartunna, many women; naṣartu, the speaker alone (al-mutakallim waḥdahu); naṣarnā, the speaker with others (al-mutakallim maʿa al-ghayr). In the print the Turkish under each form gives just this name and its meaning.

Two of the fourteen are the same word: naṣartumā serves two men and two women addressed. And naṣarnā is “we” for two or for many, men or women. So the table has fourteen places but thirteen different words, and the student learns to say which place a form stands in.

What changes is only the end. The stem naṣar- stays, and the endings are the doer pronouns you meet in naḥw: -ā, -ū, -na, -ta, -tumā, -tum, -ti, -tunna, -tu, -nā (the -at of naṣarat is the sign of the feminine, not a pronoun). Before an ending that begins with a consonant, the last letter of the stem takes a sukūn: naṣar-ta, naṣar-tu, naṣar-nā.

The same endings serve every sound verb. Only the vowel of the stem differs with the bāb: naṣara, ḍaraba and fataḥa have faʿala; samiʿa has faʿila; karuma has faʿula. Samiʿtu, “I heard”, and karumtu, “I was noble”, are built exactly like naṣartu.

lessons.title: The passive past
body: The second table is the passive past (al-māḍī al-majhūl, “the past whose doer is unknown”): nuṣira, “he was helped”, through nuṣirnā, “we were helped”. The fourteen places and their order are those of the active; only the vowels of the stem change.

The rule is short: the first letter takes a ḍamma and the letter before the last a kasra. Naṣara becomes nuṣira. Every bāb comes out the same: ḍaraba becomes ḍuriba, fataḥa futiḥa, samiʿa sumiʿa, kataba kutiba. Whatever the vowel of the active, the passive past of the bare verb is always fuʿila. In the four-letter verb the same rule gives akrama, ukrima.

The endings are the same as in the active, but they now stand for the one acted on: nuṣirtu is “I was helped”, nuṣirū “they were helped”. Naḥw calls this noun or pronoun the deputy of the doer (nāʾib al-fāʿil), since it takes the doer's place and its rafʿ.

Only a verb that takes an object has a passive with all fourteen persons. The ṣarf books give the passive tables for naṣara because naṣara takes an object and so shows the whole pattern. A verb like karuma, “to be noble”, takes no object and has no such table.

The trap is in the writing. Unvowelled, نصرت can be naṣartu, naṣarta, naṣarti, naṣarat, “I, you, you (f.), she helped”, or nuṣirtu, nuṣirta, nuṣirti, nuṣirat, the same persons “were helped”: eight readings of four letters. Only the vowels decide, and the student who recites the Amthila aloud learns to hear them.

lessons.title: The active present (muḍāriʿ)
body: The third table is the active present (al-muḍāriʿ al-maʿlūm), “he helps” or “he will help”: yanṣuru through nanṣuru, in the same fourteen places. Unlike the past, the present changes at both ends: a prefix in front and, for some persons, an ending.

The prefixes are the four letters of anaytu. Ya- for the absent man in all three numbers, and for the absent women (yanṣurna). Ta- for the absent woman and the two absent women, and for every person addressed. A- for “I” (anṣuru), na- for “we” (nanṣuru). So tanṣuru is both “she helps” and “you (a man) help”; only the context tells which.

The endings: -u for one person (yanṣuru, tanṣuru, anṣuru, nanṣuru); -āni for two (yanṣurāni, tanṣurāni); -ūna for men in the plural (yanṣurūna, tanṣurūna); -na for women in the plural (yanṣurna, tanṣurna); and -īna for the woman addressed (tanṣurīna). The forms with -āni, -ūna and -īna are the five verbs of naḥw, which keep or lose their nūn; the forms with -na have a fixed ending.

The table repeats itself: tanṣuru fills two places, the absent woman and the man addressed, and tanṣurāni three, the two absent women, the two men addressed and the two women addressed. So the fourteen places hold eleven different words. Learn the table as five rows of three, as in the grid below, and the repetitions become easy to see.

The vowel of the second root letter, the ʿayn, belongs to the bāb, not to the person: yanṣuru (u), yaḍribu (i), yaftaḥu (a), yasmaʿu (a), yakrumu (u). It is the one thing a dictionary gives for each verb, and the ṣarf books name the bābs by it: naṣara, yanṣuru; ḍaraba, yaḍribu; and so on.

lessons.title: The passive present
body: The fourth table is the passive present: yunṣaru, “he is helped”, through nunṣaru, “we are helped”. The prefixes and the endings are those of the active present; only two vowels change.

The rule: the first letter, the prefix, takes a ḍamma, and the letter before the last a fatḥa. Yanṣuru becomes yunṣaru; tanṣurūna becomes tunṣarūna; anṣuru becomes unṣaru. As with the passive past, every bāb comes out the same: yuḍrabu, yuftaḥu, yusmaʿu, yuktabu. The passive present of the bare verb is always yufʿalu.

In the four-letter verb the prefix already has a ḍamma in the active (yukrimu), so only the second vowel tells them apart: yukrimu, “he honours”, against yukramu, “he is honoured”. This one vowel is the whole difference between doing and suffering, and in unvowelled writing it disappears.

Put the four tables you have learnt side by side and the system appears: past and present, each active and passive. Nuṣira and yunṣaru share the ḍamma on the first letter, the mark of the passive; nuṣira has kasra before the last letter, yunṣaru fatḥa. The rest of the book builds on these four tables: the negations, commands and prohibitions are made from the present, active and passive.

lessons.title: The maṣdar
body: The maṣdar, the verbal noun, names the act itself without a doer or a time: naṣr, “helping, help”. The book gives it in three forms: naṣran, naṣrāni, naṣarātun: one, two and many. The heading calls it “the maṣdar that is not mīmī”, to set it apart from manṣar, the maṣdar that begins with a mīm, which comes later with the nouns of time and place.

Why the dual and the plural of an act? The maṣdar on its own names helping as such, and as such it has no number. Put in the dual or the plural, it names kinds or instances of helping: “two helpings”, “helpings”. In the plural the print vowels the ṣād with a fatḥa: naṣarāt.

In the recital of the varied forms the maṣdar is naṣran, in naṣb: naṣara, yanṣuru, naṣran. The commentaries explain it as the absolute object of the verb before it, “he helped a helping”. In its own table only the first word keeps that naṣb; the dual and the plural are given as plain nouns.

The maṣdar of the bare verb is learnt by hearing, not by rule (samāʿī). Naṣara has naṣr, ḍaraba has ḍarb, qatala has qatl, as the Ājurrūmiyya's examples show, but other verbs have other shapes, and the dictionary gives them. That is why the conjugation tool leaves the maṣdar of the bare verb empty. The augmented verbs have regular maṣdars: akrama, ikrām; the Binā and al-ʿIzzī give their patterns.

lessons.title: The active participle
body: The active participle (ism al-fāʿil, “the noun of the doer”) names or describes the one who does the act: nāṣir, “one who helps, a helper”. In the bare verb its pattern is fāʿil: an alif after the first letter and a kasra under the second. In the recital it is fa-huwa nāṣirun, “so he is a helper”.

The table gives it in all its numbers and both genders. Masculine: nāṣir, the dual nāṣirāni, the sound plural nāṣirūna, and three broken plurals, nuṣṣār, nuṣṣar and naṣara. Feminine: nāṣira, nāṣiratāni, nāṣirāt, and the broken plural nawāṣir. The wāw the print puts before some of the broken plurals (wa-nuṣṣarun, wa-naṣaratun, wa-nawāṣiru) marks them as further plurals of the same word.

The sound plurals are formed by rule; the broken plurals, as always in Arabic, are learnt. The Amthila gives three patterns for the men, fuʿʿāl, fuʿʿal and faʿala, and one for the women, fawāʿil. Al-ʿIzzī and Marāḥ al-arwāḥ return to them.

For every sound bare verb the participle is fāʿil: ḍārib (striking), fātiḥ (opening), sāmiʿ (hearing), kātib (writing). For the augmented verbs it begins with mu- and has a kasra before the last letter: akrama gives mukrim, “one who honours”. Naḥw adds that the participle can work like its verb: nāṣirun Zaydan, “helping Zayd”, with Zayd as its object.

A trap of the table: naṣara, the third broken plural, “helpers”, is written and vowelled exactly like the past verb naṣara, “he helped”. Only its place in the sentence, and its tanwīn (naṣaratun), show that it is a noun.

lessons.title: The passive participle
body: The passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl, “the noun of the one acted on”) names or describes the one to whom the act is done: manṣūr, “helped, one who is helped”. In the bare verb its pattern is mafʿūl: a mīm before the root and a long ū before the last letter. In the recital it is wa-dhāka manṣūrun, “and that one is helped”.

The table gives manṣūr, manṣūrāni, manṣūrūna for the men, manṣūra, manṣūratāni, manṣūrāt for the women, and one broken plural, manāṣir (mafāʿil). It is shorter than the table of the active participle: the passive participle is mostly made plural by rule.

For every sound bare verb the pattern is the same: maḍrūb (struck), maftūḥ (opened), masmūʿ (heard), maktūb (written). For the augmented verbs it begins with mu-, like the active participle, but has a fatḥa before the last letter: mukram, “honoured”, against mukrim, “one who honours”. One vowel again divides the doer from the one acted on, as in yukrimu and yukramu.

As with the passive verbs, only a verb with an object has a passive participle of its own. And a beginner's trap: maktūb also means “a letter” and manṣūr is also a man's name. A participle easily becomes an ordinary noun; ṣarf names its form, and the sentence shows its use.

lessons.title: The absolute denial: lam
body: The negations begin with lam: lam yanṣur, “he did not help”. Lam is followed by the present, but it turns its meaning to the past, and it puts the verb in jazm. The Ottoman books call this form the absolute denial (al-jaḥd al-muṭlaq): the act is denied in the past, with no limit set on when.

The table is the present table with lam before each form, and three things happen to the endings. The single forms lose their -u and end in sukūn: lam yanṣur, lam tanṣur, lam anṣur, lam nanṣur. The five verbs lose their nūn: lam yanṣurā, lam yanṣurū, lam tanṣurī. The forms of the women keep their -na, which never changes: lam yanṣurna, lam tanṣurna.

The passive table (p. 241–242) does the same with the passive present: lam yunṣar, “he was not helped”, lam yunṣarū, “they were not helped”, lam unṣar, “I was not helped”. Prefix with ḍamma, fatḥa before the last letter, and the endings of jazm.

The same holds for every sound verb: lam yaḍrib, lam yaktub, lam yasmaʿ, lam yaḍribū. A beginner sometimes puts lam before the past, lam naṣara; that is wrong. Lam always takes the form of the present, and the past meaning comes from lam itself. To deny with the past form one says mā naṣara, “he did not help”, which the Amthila does not teach.

lessons.title: The comprehensive denial: lammā
body: The second negation is lammā: lammā yanṣur, “he has not yet helped”. Its forms are those of lam exactly, the present in jazm: lammā yanṣur, lammā yanṣurū, lammā yanṣurna, and in the passive lammā yunṣar. Only its meaning is different.

The Ottoman books call it the comprehensive denial (al-jaḥd al-mustaghriq): it takes in the whole of the past right up to the moment of speaking, and leaves open that the act may still happen. Lam yanṣur may speak of a past now closed (“he did not help that day”); lammā yanṣur says “up to now he has not helped, and one waits for it”.

The Qurʾān shows the sense: wa-lammā yadkhuli al-īmānu fī qulūbikum, “faith has not yet entered your hearts” (Q 49:14). Faith has not entered up to now, and it is expected. The sukūn of yadkhul takes a kasra there only to join the next word.

A trap: lammā followed by a past verb is another word altogether, the lammā of time, “when”: lammā jāʾa Zaydun, “when Zayd came”. It governs nothing. The lammā of the Amthila always comes before a present verb, and puts it in jazm.

lammā of time, “when”, before the past

tasks.answer: Lammā yaktub, lammā yaktubū, lammā taktubī, lammā aktub.

tasks.prompt: Translate lam yaktub and lammā yaktub and explain the difference.
tasks.answer: Lam yaktub: “he did not write”, a denial in the past without saying more. Lammā yaktub: “he has not yet written”, the denial reaches up to now and the writing is still expected.

lessons.title: The negations of the present and the future: mā and lā
body: Two negations change nothing in the verb. Mā yanṣuru, “he is not helping”, is the negation of the present (nafy al-ḥāl); lā yanṣuru, “he will not help”, is the negation of the future (nafy al-istiqbāl). Their four tables, active and passive, are simply the present tables with mā or lā before each form.

Since neither governs the verb, every ending stays: the -u (mā yanṣuru, lā anṣuru), and the nūn of the five verbs (mā yanṣurāni, lā yanṣurūna, lā tanṣurīna). Set this beside lam, lammā and lan, which all change the ending, and the five negations fall into two groups: those that govern and those that do not.

The Amthila gives each negation one time, so that the student can tell the five apart: lam and lammā for the past, mā for the present, lā and lan for the future. Naḥw adds more. Lā before the present can also deny the present, and mā can also stand before the past, mā naṣara, “he did not help”. The scheme of the Amthila is a first map, not the whole country.

The great trap of this lesson is the lā of prohibition, which looks the same. Lā yanṣuru, with ḍamma, is a negation: “he will not help”. Lā yanṣur, with sukūn, is a prohibition: “let him not help”. In the second person the difference is even sharper: lā tanṣuru, “you will not help”, against lā tanṣur, “do not help!”. One vowel separates a statement from an order.
The passive tables follow the same rule on the passive present: mā yunṣaru, “he is not being helped”, lā yunṣaru, “he will not be helped”, with all the endings kept.

the negation of the future: lā yanṣuru
the lā of negation, which governs nothing
the lā of prohibition, which puts the verb in jazm

tasks.prompt: Put mā and lā before these forms of kataba and translate: yaktubu, yaktubūna, taktubīna.
tasks.answer: Mā yaktubu “he is not writing”, lā yaktubu “he will not write”; mā yaktubūna, lā yaktubūna “they are not writing, will not write”; mā taktubīna, lā taktubīna “you (a woman) are not writing, will not write”. No ending changes.

tasks.answer: Mā yunṣarūna; lā tunṣarīna.

tasks.prompt: Which of the five negations change the ending of the verb, and how?
tasks.answer: Lam and lammā put it in jazm (sukūn, or the nūn dropped); lan puts it in naṣb (fatḥa, or the nūn dropped). Mā and lā change nothing.

quiz.explanation: Mā yanṣuru: the ḍamma stays.

quiz.prompt: Which time does the Amthila give to lā yanṣuru?
quiz.explanation: Nafy al-istiqbāl: “he will not help”.

quiz.prompt: Lā tanṣur, with sukūn, means…
quiz.explanation: The lā of prohibition puts the verb in jazm.

quiz.prompt: Lā tanṣurīna means…
quiz.explanation: The nūn stays: it is a negation, not a prohibition (that would be lā tanṣurī).

quiz.prompt: Which negations govern the verb?
quiz.explanation: Mā and lā leave the ending as it is.

quiz.prompt: Can mā also come before a past verb?

quiz.explanation: Naḥw allows it; the Amthila gives mā one use to keep the scheme simple.

quiz.prompt: “He will not be helped” is…
quiz.explanation: Lā with the passive present, the ending kept.

lessons.title: The emphatic negation of the future: lan
body: The last negation is lan: lan yanṣura, “he will never help”, “he will certainly not help”. The Ottoman books call it the emphatic negation of the future (taʾkīd nafy al-istiqbāl): what lā yanṣuru says, lan yanṣura says more strongly.

Lan governs the verb and puts it in naṣb. The single forms take a fatḥa: lan yanṣura, lan tanṣura, lan anṣura, lan nanṣura. The five verbs drop their nūn: lan yanṣurā, lan yanṣurū, lan tanṣurī. The forms of the women keep their -na: lan yanṣurna, lan tanṣurna.

Now compare lam. Both drop the nūn of the five verbs, so lam yanṣurū and lan yanṣurū are written and said alike, the first in jazm (“they did not help”), the second in naṣb (“they will never help”). Only the particle tells them apart. In the single forms the two differ: lam yanṣur, sukūn; lan yanṣura, fatḥa.

The passive table gives lan yunṣara, “he will never be helped”, through lan nunṣara. The Qurʾān has the active of the speaker: fa-lan abraḥa al-arḍa, “I will not leave the land” (Q 12:80), abraḥa in naṣb after lan.

lessons.title: Command and prohibition to the absent
body: To order or forbid someone who is not addressed, Arabic uses the present with a particle. The command to the absent (amr al-ghāʾib) is li- with the present in jazm: li-yanṣur, “let him help”, li-yanṣurū, “let them help”. The prohibition to the absent (nahy al-ghāʾib) is lā with the present in jazm: lā yanṣur, “let him not help”, lā yanṣurū, “let them not help”.

The endings are those of lam: sukūn in the single forms, the nūn dropped in the five verbs, the -na of the women kept (li-yanṣurna, lā yanṣurna). The lām of command takes a kasra; after wa- or fa- it loses its vowel, as in fa-l-yanṣur, “so let him help”.

In this print the active tables give the six absent persons only, three of the men and three of the women. The passive tables give eight: the six absent with the passive present, li-yunṣar, “let him be helped”, lā yunṣar, “let him not be helped”, and two more for the speaker, li-unṣar, “let me be helped”, li-nunṣar, “let us be helped”, and lā unṣar, lā nunṣar.
Remember the trap of the lā. In the prohibition the verb is in jazm: lā yanṣur, lā yanṣurū. In the negation it keeps its ending: lā yanṣuru, lā yanṣurūna. The first orders, the second only states.

lessons.title: Command and prohibition to the one present
body: To the person addressed the command has a form of its own, the imperative: unṣur, unṣurā, unṣurū, unṣurī, unṣurā, unṣurna: “help!” to a man, to two, to men, to a woman, to two women, to women. This is the command to the one present (amr al-ḥāḍir).

It is made from the present of the second person. Take tanṣuru, drop the prefix ta-, and the word now begins with a letter that has no vowel, which Arabic cannot say; so a hamza is put in front, with a ḍamma when the ʿayn has a ḍamma (unṣur, uktub) and a kasra when it has a kasra or a fatḥa (iḍrib, iftaḥ, ismaʿ). The end is that of jazm: sukūn, the nūn dropped, the -na kept. The print writes the hamza on an alif with a ḍamma: اُنْصُرْ.

This hamza is a hamza of joining (waṣl): it is said only at the start of speech and drops after another word. The Qurʾān has fa-nṣurnā ʿalā al-qawmi al-kāfirīna, “so help us against the unbelieving people” (Q 2:286), where after fa- no hamza is heard. In the four-letter verb the hamza is part of the pattern and is always said, with a fatḥa: akrim, “honour!”.

The passive has no imperative form, so the book uses the lām of command with the passive present: li-tunṣar, “be helped!”, li-tunṣarū, and adds li-unṣar and li-nunṣar for the speaker. The prohibition to the one present is lā with the present in jazm, in the active lā tanṣur, “do not help!”, through lā tanṣurna, and in the passive lā tunṣar, “do not be helped”, with lā unṣar and lā nunṣar.

With this the verb tables are complete: past and present, each active and passive, five negations, and command and prohibition to the absent and to the present. Every one of them has been made from the four tables of lessons 3 to 6.

lessons.title: The nouns of time, place and instrument
body: The last part of the book gives the nouns made from the verb, each in its own small table. The first is manṣar: manṣar, manṣarāni, manāṣir. The heading names three things at once: the noun of time (“a time of helping”), the noun of place (“a place of helping”) and the maṣdar mīmī (“a helping”). One form, three uses; the sentence decides which.

Its pattern is mafʿal: a mīm before the root and a fatḥa before the last letter. The ṣarf books give the rule: the noun of time and place is mafʿal when the present has a ḍamma or a fatḥa on the ʿayn (yanṣuru, yaftaḥu), and mafʿil when it has a kasra (yaḍribu, yajlisu), as in the familiar majlis, “a place of sitting”. The maṣdar mīmī of the sound bare verb is mafʿal in every bāb.

The noun of instrument (ism al-āla) is minṣar: minṣar, minṣarāni, manāṣir: “a thing to help with”. Its pattern here is mifʿal; the books add two more, mifʿāl and mifʿala, which many common words show: miftāḥ, “a key”, the thing to open with.

Look at the two tables together: manṣar and minṣar differ only by the vowel of the mīm, fatḥa for time and place, kasra for the instrument, and their broken plurals are the same, manāṣir. In such a case only the singular, or the sentence, shows which noun is meant.

lessons.title: One act and its manner: marra and nawʿ
body: Two forms count or qualify the act. The form of once (bināʾ al-marra) is naṣra: naṣra, naṣratāni, naṣarāt, “one act of helping, two, several”. Its pattern is faʿla. The form of the manner (bināʾ al-nawʿ) is niṣra: niṣra, niṣratāni, niṣarāt, “a way of helping”. Its pattern is fiʿla.

Both are made on the maṣdar and differ from it, and from each other, by small marks: naṣr, the act as such; naṣra, with a tāʾ, the act counted once; niṣra, with a kasra and a tāʾ, the act of a certain kind. In both plurals the print vowels the ṣād with a fatḥa: naṣarāt, niṣarāt.

In the sentence they serve as the absolute object of the Ājurrūmiyya (its lesson 26), which shows the number or the kind of the act: naṣartuhu naṣratan, “I helped him once”; naṣartuhu naṣratayni, “twice”; naṣartuhu niṣratan, “I helped him in a certain way”, usually followed by a word that says which way.

The trap: naṣra and niṣra are one vowel apart, as manṣar and minṣar were. And the tāʾ of naṣra is the round tāʾ of a noun, vowelled and with tanwīn (naṣratun), not the quiescent tāʾ of the past verb naṣarat.

lessons.title: The diminutive and the relative adjective
body: The diminutive (ism al-taṣghīr) makes a noun small: nuṣayr, “a little help”, with its dual nuṣayrāni and plural nuṣayrūna; this print gives only these three. The pattern is fuʿayl: a ḍamma on the first letter, a fatḥa on the second, and a yāʾ with sukūn added after it. The commentaries add that the diminutive can also show endearment or slight, and many Arabic names are diminutives: ʿUmayr from ʿAmr, Zuhayr from Zahr.

The relative adjective (al-ism al-mansūb, the nisba) makes a noun into an adjective, “related to”, “of”: naṣrī, “related to help”, by adding a doubled yāʾ, -iyy. The table gives both genders and three numbers: naṣrī, naṣriyyāni, naṣriyyūna; naṣriyya, naṣriyyatāni, naṣriyyāt. The same ending makes Makkī, “from Makka”, and ʿArabī, “Arab, Arabic”.

Both are made on a noun, not on the verb: nuṣayr and naṣrī start from naṣr, the maṣdar. The Amthila puts them here because it gathers on one root every pattern a student will meet, verbs and nouns alike.

Do not confuse the nisba's -iyy with the -ī of “my”: naṣrī can be read naṣriyy, “related to help”, or naṣrī, “my help”. The doubled yāʾ (written with a shadda) and tanwīn, naṣriyyun, show the adjective.

lessons.title: The intensive and the elative
body: The intensive of the active participle (mubālaghat ism al-fāʿil) describes one who does the act much or often: naṣṣār, “a great helper”. Its pattern here is faʿʿāl, with the ʿayn doubled and a long ā; the table gives naṣṣār, naṣṣārāni, naṣṣārūna for the men and naṣṣāra, naṣṣāratāni, naṣṣārāt for the women. The books name other patterns of the intensive too, such as faʿūl and faʿīl; the divine names al-Ghaffār, al-Ghafūr and al-Raḥīm are all intensives.

The elative (ism al-tafḍīl, “the noun of preference”) says that one has more of a quality than another: anṣar, “more helpful”, “most helpful”. Its pattern is afʿal for the man, with the dual anṣarāni and the plurals anṣarūna and anāṣir; and fuʿlā for the woman, nuṣrā, with nuṣrayāni, nuṣrayāt and nuṣar.

Naḥw gives the use. Followed by min, “than”, the elative stays as it is, whoever it describes: Zaydun anṣaru min ʿAmrin, “Zayd is more helpful than ʿAmr”, and the same anṣaru for a woman or for many. The feminine and plural forms are used with the article or in iḍāfa: al-nuṣrā, “the most helpful (woman)”.

The familiar pairs show the pattern: akbar and kubrā, “greater, greatest”, aṣghar and ṣughrā, “smaller, smallest”, which the madrasa knows from book titles such as al-Ṣughrā and al-Kubrā. The elative anṣaru is a diptote: in khafḍ it takes a fatḥa, without tanwīn.

lessons.title: The two verbs of wonder
body: The book ends with the two verbs of wonder (taʿajjub), each in fourteen places. The first is mā afʿalahu: mā anṣarahu, “how helpful he is!”. The second is afʿil bihi: anṣir bihi, which means the same. In both, the verb never changes; only the pronoun of the one wondered at moves through the persons: mā anṣarahu, mā anṣarahumā, mā anṣarahum … mā anṣaranī, mā anṣaranā; anṣir bihi, anṣir bihimā … anṣir bī, anṣir binā.

Naḥw explains the parts. In mā anṣarahu, mā is a noun at the head of the sentence, which the Baṣrans explain as “something great”; anṣara is a past verb on the pattern afʿala, with a hidden pronoun as its doer; -hu is its object, the one wondered at. Literally, “something great has made him helpful”. That is why the pronoun is an object pronoun: mā anṣaranī, with the nūn of protection, “how helpful I am!”.

The second form, anṣir bihi, is an imperative in shape but a statement in meaning. It is fixed: one does not say anṣirū bihim for many; the bi- and its pronoun carry all the change. The print joins every form to the recital with wa-: wa-anṣir bihi.
The Qurʾān uses both: qutila al-insānu mā akfarahu, “perish man! how ungrateful he is!” (Q 80:17), and asmiʿ bihim wa-abṣir, “how well they will hear and see!” (Q 19:38).

With this the Amthila is complete: one verb, laid out in every form a beginner needs, recited aloud until it is known. In the Ottoman madrasa the Binā and the Maqṣūd come next, which explain how these forms are built and how the other bābs and patterns follow them; al-ʿIzzī and Marāḥ al-arwāḥ take the same matter further.
